title: Al-Jalil, the Majestic
tomorrow: what does Dadi slip into Amira's bag before she asks?

lines: A STORM. AN OCEAN. A CEILING.
cards: A thunderstorm rolling over the freeway. The ocean at night, louder than you expected. The reading room of a huge library, ceilings so high your voice drops on its own.
Something in you goes quiet and small. Amira felt it yesterday, in a university library with her dad, craning her neck. Is that awe, or just a polite word for fear?
Muslim scholars have given two answers, and both are worth hearing. The Name at the center is Al-Jalil, the Majestic.

teach.h: LORD OF MAJESTY AND GENEROUS HONOR.
teach.b: The Qur'an pictures that majesty in Surah Ar-Rahman. Everyone on the earth passes away. "There remaineth but the Countenance of thy Lord of Might and Glory."
In Arabic, the phrase is dhul-jalali wal-ikram: the Lord of majesty, and of generous honor.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: TREMBLING GUARDS THE HEART.
teach.b: Here's the first view. Majesty should make you tremble, and the trembling is a gift. Surah Al-Anfal describes the believers as those "whose hearts feel fear when Allah is mentioned."
Scholars who lean this way say a heart that feels that fear is guarded: it stops before doing what it would regret. Awe that never shakes you, they'd say, hasn't really seen anything.
It's like standing at a cliff edge: you step back, and you're glad you did. Now the second view. Look again at that phrase: majesty and generous honor, side by side, never majesty alone.
Scholars who lean this way point to a hadith in Sahih Muslim: let none of you die except thinking well of Allah. For them, majesty that only frightens has been heard halfway.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: AWE PULLS YOU CLOSER.
teach.b: Real awe pulls you closer, the way you lean toward the ocean, not away from it.
Some scholars hold both, and say fear and hope are like the two wings of a bird: lose either one, and you can't fly. Here's something to tell a friend tonight.
A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi tells Muslims to hold on to the call ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram in their du'a: majesty and generosity, said in one breath.

how: Muslims call on Allah as ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram, Lord of majesty and generous honor, in du'a; scholars have long weighed khawf (fear) and raja' (hope) in a believer's heart, and some describe them as two wings.

o: the one who judges the proud at the gate
the Majestic, whose greatness fills you with awe
the one who sends storms to warn a city

games.q: two views, one Name — tap the pairs.

s: in Surah Ar-Rahman, God's majesty stands alone, with nothing softer beside it
dhul-jalali wal-ikram: majesty paired with generous honor (55:27).
Muslim scholars all agree awe should mainly be fear
some lean toward fear, some toward hope; some say both, like two wings of a bird.
a hadith in Sahih Muslim says to die thinking well of Allah
it's one of the texts the hope side leans on.

games.q: you lean toward the hope view: majesty draws you closer. Jordan pushes back. what's the strongest case for the fear view, put the way its scholars would?
o: 'a heart that trembles at His majesty is guarded from what it would regret.'
'fear is right because God is mostly angry with people.'
'awe and fear are the same thing, so there's nothing to debate.'
games.why: at its best the fear view isn't gloomy: 8:2 ties a trembling heart to belief, and the trembling protects. the hope view answers with 55:27's pairing and the hadith in Muslim. some scholars keep both wings.

practice: Stand up, feet planted, and stretch both arms out as wide as they go. Hold the stretch for three slow breaths, and notice the room around your hands, and all that lies past the walls.
Notice whether you feel small, or held, or both. Then lower your arms and sit down for the bell.

wordCard.voice: Al-Jalil. The Majestic, whose majesty the Qur'an pairs with generous honor. Name forty-one.

orig.note: Arabic: the Majestic. the Qur'an's phrase is dhul-jalali wal-ikram, Lord of majesty and generous honor (55:27).

carryVoice: Carry this: majesty, big enough to shake you and close enough to lean toward. That's forty-one.
